This article walks through a modeling project with balancedsample: a balanced training/testing split, balanced folds on the training set, tuning with tune, and a final fit. It also shows how to choose the columns to balance, how to check the result, and how to choose a method.

## The data

The package includes `sim_patients`, a simulated data set of 300 patients at three sites. Age and income are skewed, and diagnosis has a rare level. The outcome depends on age, income, and diagnosis. `?sim_patients` gives the formula.

```{r data}
library(balancedsample)

d <- sim_patients
n <- nrow(d)
head(d)
```

The splits are random, so set a seed to get the same splits each time:

```{r seed}
set.seed(2026)
```

## Why balance?

In tidymodels, a modeling project usually starts with `rsample::initial_split()`, which holds out a test set, and `rsample::vfold_cv()`, which makes cross-validation folds from the training set. Both take `strata`, which stratifies on one column: each set gets about the same share of each of its levels. (By default, a numeric column with more than five distinct values is first cut into up to four bins. Otherwise, the rows of levels with under 10% of the rows are spread at random over the other levels.) But what if you want the sets to be similar on several variables at once? Here, we might want every fold to have similar ages, incomes, diagnoses, and sites. With 300 rows and 10 folds, each held-out fold has only about 30 rows, so folds stratified on diagnosis alone can still differ on the other variables, as the output below shows.

Why does this matter? Each held-out set stands in for new data. If one fold has older patients or more severe cases than the rest, its score reflects that difference as well as the model. Random folds can differ like this by chance. That makes a single cross-validation estimate less accurate, and more repeats are needed to get a stable one ([Moreno-Torres et al., 2012](https://doi.org/10.1109/TNNLS.2012.2199516)). In [Kohavi's (1995)](https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/95-2/Papers/016.pdf) tests, folds stratified on the outcome class gave estimates with slightly less bias and variance than plain random folds. Folds that also matched on the predictors gave less biased estimates, especially with few folds ([Zeng and Martinez, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1080/095281300146272); [Diamantidis et al., 2000](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0004-3702%2899%2900094-6)). For a training/testing split, sets that each look like the whole data made poor test results less likely than random splits did ([Joseph and Vakayil, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.2021.1921037)).

The gains are largest when the sets are small and, for a yes/no outcome, when each set has few events. `balance_check()` doesn't tell you how much balancing will gain. It shows how balanced the sets are compared with random sets of the same sizes, and random folds can look unbalanced without costing much.

In one simulation study, 10-fold cross-validation of a random forest was run with balanced folds (balancing on the predictors, with the outcome in `exact`) and with random folds. One set of balanced folds gave an estimate as steady as the average over 1.8 to 4.2 sets of random folds with about 5 rows per fold, 1.2 to 11 with 10 rows per fold (the high end with 5% events, under 1 event per fold), 1.0 to 3.1 with 30 rows per fold, and about 1 (no gain) with 100 rows per fold. The typical error against the model fit to all the data was at most about 9% smaller, for AUC with folds of 30 rows or fewer, and within 2% for the Brier score and RMSE. So balancing is worth most with small folds and rare events, and with folds of 100 rows or more it changes little.

Balanced folds also differ less from each other, so the standard error that tune reports for a metric tends to be smaller. That standard error is a rough guide at best, because the folds share training rows and no formula from the fold scores gets it right in general ([Bengio and Grandvalet, 2004](https://jmlr.org/papers/v5/grandvalet04a.html)). A smaller value is not proof of a better estimate. Last, balancing makes the held-out rows look like the rest. If the model will be used at new sites or in later periods, the held-out rows should differ in that way instead (see [Choosing columns](#choosing-columns-balance-and-exact)).

`balance_check()` measures how similar the sets are. For each fold, it compares the held-out rows with the other rows in two ways:

- The standardized mean difference (SMD) is computed for each variable on its own. It is the difference in means (held-out rows minus the other rows) divided by the pooled standard deviation. For a categorical variable, there is one SMD per level, from the proportions of that level. An absolute SMD under 0.1 is a common rule of thumb for good balance, but random sets rarely meet it when they are small or when many variables are checked.
- The energy distance compares all the variables at once. It turns each level of a categorical variable into a 0/1 column, standardizes all the columns, and then looks at the distances between rows. It is twice the average distance between a row of one set and a row of the other, minus the average distance between two rows of the same set (once for each set, counting each row paired with itself). It is 0 when the two sets have the same distribution, and it grows as they differ. Unlike the SMD, it also picks up differences in spread and shape, and in how the variables relate to each other. It has no fixed cutoff like 0.1, so use it to compare splits of the same data on the same variables.

To tell balance from chance, `balance_check()` also deals the rows of each fold out at random into two sets of the same sizes, 100 times by default (set `chance`), and measures each variable the same way. This shows how random sets of the same sizes from these data would look.

For each fold, `balance_check()` returns one SMD row per numeric variable, one per level of each categorical variable, and one energy row. Printing the result shows one row per fold. Each variable first counts with its largest absolute SMD, so a variable with three levels counts once, like a numeric one. The row then gives the largest absolute SMD and the variable it belongs to, the mean over the variables, and that mean divided by the same mean in the random sets (`vs chance`). Random folds give about 1 and balanced folds less. Next comes how many variables are above what 95% of the random sets stay under (`over chance`), and last the energy distance. `summary()` returns the same numbers as a tibble. The largest SMD shows which variable to look at. The mean is steadier for comparing splits, because the largest grows with the number of variables checked. Here are ordinary folds from rsample, stratified on diagnosis. For these, you list the columns to check:

```{r random}
random_folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(d, v = 10, strata = diagnosis)
random_check <- balance_check(random_folds, age, income, diagnosis, site)
random_check
```

And here are balanced folds. `balance` lists the columns to make similar, and `exact` takes the place of `strata`. The next section explains both. Balanced folds remember these columns, so `balance_check()` needs no column list:

```{r balanced}
folds <- balanced_vfold_cv(
  d,
  v = 10,
  balance = c(age, income),
  exact = c(diagnosis, site)
)
balanced_check <- balance_check(folds)
balanced_check
```

```{r compare, include = FALSE}
random_sum <- summary(random_check)
balanced_sum <- summary(balanced_check)
severe_n <- vapply(
  folds$splits,
  function(s) sum(rsample::assessment(s)$diagnosis == "severe"),
  integer(1)
)
```

The largest absolute SMD in any fold fell from `r round(max(random_sum$max_abs_smd), 2)` to `r round(max(balanced_sum$max_abs_smd), 2)`, the mean absolute SMD over folds fell from `r round(mean(random_sum$mean_abs_smd), 3)` to `r round(mean(balanced_sum$mean_abs_smd), 3)`, the mean ratio to chance fell from `r round(mean(random_sum$ratio_to_chance), 2)` (under 1 already, because these folds are stratified on diagnosis) to `r round(mean(balanced_sum$ratio_to_chance), 2)`, and the mean energy distance fell from `r round(mean(random_sum$energy), 3)` to `r round(mean(balanced_sum$energy), 3)`. With `by = "variable"`, `summary()` shows where what is left comes from:

```{r by-variable}
summary(balanced_check, by = "variable")
```

It is mostly in the category proportions of the `exact` columns. The counts are rounded for each combination of diagnosis and site, not for each level on its own. So a level's total in a fold can be one row off for each site, even when the total divides evenly into 10 folds. For example, the `r sum(d$diagnosis == "severe")` severe cases get `r min(severe_n)` to `r max(severe_n)` per fold. In a fold of 30 rows, one row more or less of a level moves its SMD by 0.075 to 0.11 for the levels here, so 0.1 is not always within reach. That is still well under chance: compare the `chance_q95` column, which is what the variable's largest SMD stayed under in 95% of the random sets.

## Choosing columns: `balance` and `exact`

`balance` takes numeric and categorical columns. To compare the sets, the method turns each level of a categorical column into a 0/1 column and standardizes all the columns. This happens only inside the method: your data and the splits keep the original columns. The method then makes the sets as similar as it can on all of these columns at once. This is a goal, not a rule, so the method may trade a little balance on one column for more balance on another.

`exact` takes categorical columns and is a rule. Each combination of levels is one stratum. In each set, the count of each stratum is its share of that set, rounded up or down to a whole row. This is fixed before the method runs, so it holds for every method.

`exact` does the job of `strata` in rsample, with two differences. It can take several columns, which it crosses, and its counts are exact rather than approximate. If you write `strata` out of habit, balancedsample stops and tells you to use `exact`.

A categorical column can go in either argument. Use `exact` when you need the counts as close as whole rows allow. Use `balance` when close is enough. In the folds above, diagnosis is in `exact` because the outcome depends on it, and severe cases are rare. Site is in `exact` so that each site is represented in proportion in every fold, and later in the test set. If a slightly uneven mix of sites were fine, site could go in `balance` instead.

Continuous columns belong in `balance`. If you need exact counts within ranges of a continuous column, make a factor of those ranges and put that in `exact`. Base R has `cut()`. In the tidyverse, `ggplot2::cut_number()` makes ranges with about the same number of rows, and `ggplot2::cut_interval()` and `ggplot2::cut_width()` make ranges of the same width. `dplyr::ntile()` also works: it returns whole numbers, which `exact` treats as categories.

What about the outcome? In rsample, `strata` is usually the outcome, so that every set has a similar mix of outcomes. You can do the same here. A numeric outcome can go in `balance`, next to the predictors, and a class outcome can go in `exact` if the class counts matter and every class has enough rows for every set. The outcome is used only to assign rows to sets, as with `strata`. With `method = "twinning"`, though, leave the outcome out of both. Twinning puts rows that are close on every column into different sets. With the outcome among those columns, each held-out row then has a training row much like it, outcome included. Models that predict from nearby rows, such as k-nearest neighbours, SVMs, and random forests, then score better than they will on new data. In simulations with 300 rows and 10 folds, a class outcome in `exact` raised the AUC of these models by about 0.01 to 0.04 over random folds, above their true AUC. anticlust doesn't pair rows like this: with it, the outcome changed the AUC by less than 0.005. This assumes you have the outcome when you make the split. If the evaluation must hold out whole time periods or whole sites, split by those instead: put the site in `group`, or use rsample's time-based splits. In this article, the outcome is left out. It depends on age, income, and diagnosis, so balancing those also balances the part of the outcome they explain. The rest is random noise, so the outcome itself can still differ between the sets.

Each column you add to `exact` splits the strata further. Here diagnosis and site together make 9 strata:

```{r crossed}
tab <- table(d$diagnosis, d$site)
tab
```

```{r smallest, include = FALSE}
small <- which(tab == min(tab), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
small_train <- round(0.8 * min(tab))
```

The smallest stratum is `r rownames(tab)[small[1]]` cases at site `r colnames(tab)[small[2]]`, with `r min(tab)` patients. After an 80% training split, `r small_train` of them are spread over 5 folds, so each fold gets `r floor(small_train / 5)` or `r ceiling(small_train / 5)`. A stratum with fewer rows than folds is missing from some folds. Small strata also leave the method less room to balance the other columns.

### Missing values

By default, the columns in `balance`, `exact`, and `group` must not have missing values. With `na = "include"`, the rows with missing values stay in, and the method also balances which values are missing. Here, 30 incomes and 15 sites are missing:

```{r missing}
d_na <- d
d_na$income[sample(n, 30)] <- NA
d_na$site[sample(n, 15)] <- NA
folds_na <- balanced_vfold_cv(
  d_na,
  v = 10,
  balance = c(age, income),
  exact = c(diagnosis, site),
  na = "include"
)
```

Each column type is handled in its own way:

- In a numeric `balance` column such as income, the missing values get the mean of the observed values, and a 0/1 column of which values are missing is balanced too. Once the share missing is balanced, balancing the filled column also balances the mean of the observed incomes. The filled values all sit at the mean, so the spread of the observed incomes is balanced less closely.
- In a categorical `balance` column, a missing value is one more level.
- In an `exact` column such as site, a missing value is one more level too. The counts are exact for each combination of diagnosis and site, so the 15 rows are spread over the folds within each diagnosis. Their total in a fold can still be one row off for each diagnosis, so some folds get more of the 15 than others, and the `"(missing)"` SMD of site can be large. With `group`, a group with some rows at site A and some with a missing site is an error, because a missing value counts as a level of its own.

These encodings are used only to make the split. The data in the folds keep their missing values, so your model can handle them its own way, for example with a recipe.

`balance_check()` adds a row with `level` `"(missing)"` for each column with missing values. It gives the SMD of the share of values that are missing. In the summaries, it counts as one more level of its column. The other SMDs use the observed values only. The energy distance uses all rows, encoded as above.

```{r missing-check}
na_check <- balance_check(folds_na)
na_rows <- tibble::as_tibble(na_check)
head(na_rows[na_rows$level %in% "(missing)", ], 4)
na_check
```

A column with no observed values is an error. A `group` column must not have missing values even with `na = "include"`, because rows with a missing ID could come from one unit or from several. Give them their own IDs, or one shared ID, depending on which is true. For a character ID column `id`:

```{r missing-group, eval = FALSE}
# One group per row with a missing ID
d$id[is.na(d$id)] <- paste0("unknown_", seq_len(sum(is.na(d$id))))
# Or one group for all of them
d$id[is.na(d$id)] <- "unknown"
```

To fill in another way, for example with the median, make the filled copy and the 0/1 column yourself and put both in `balance`.

## A full tidymodels workflow

Start with a balanced training/testing split, with the same columns as above. Then make balanced folds from the training set only, so the test set plays no part in tuning.

```{r split}
split <- balanced_initial_split(
  d,
  prop = 0.8,
  balance = c(age, income),
  exact = c(diagnosis, site)
)
train <- rsample::training(split)
balance_check(split)
```

For a single split, the table shows the signed SMD of each variable and level, and what each variable's largest SMD stayed under in 95% of random sets (`chance 95%`). The header gives the ratio to chance and the energy distance.

To tune on one validation set instead of folds, use `balanced_initial_validation_split()`, which makes a balanced training/validation/testing split. Pass it to `rsample::validation_set()` to get an `rset` for tune.

```{r folds}
folds <- balanced_vfold_cv(
  train,
  v = 5,
  balance = c(age, income),
  exact = c(diagnosis, site)
)
```

Use `autoplot()` to see the SMD of every variable in every fold. The grey band around each variable shows how far its largest SMD went in 95% of random sets of the same sizes.

```{r plot}
library(ggplot2)
autoplot(balance_check(folds))
```

The diagnosis levels sit farther from 0 than age and income, even though diagnosis is in `exact`, but they stay well inside the band. The counts are exact for each diagnosis and site combination. A fold can be one row off in each of the three sites, and these rows add up for the diagnosis as a whole. Rare levels show this most, because one row is a large share of a small level.

The folds work with tune like any other `rset`, as long as balancedsample is attached with `library()`, as in the chunk below. tune finds the function that made the folds by its name, so it fails if you only call `balancedsample::balanced_vfold_cv()`.

This example tunes the depth and the minimum node size of a decision tree:

```{r tune, message = FALSE}
library(balancedsample)
library(parsnip)
library(tune)
library(workflows)

wf <- workflow(
  outcome ~ age + income + diagnosis + site,
  decision_tree(
    tree_depth = tune(),
    min_n = tune(),
    mode = "regression"
  )
)
res <- tune_grid(wf, resamples = folds, grid = 6)
show_best(res, metric = "rmse", n = 3)
```

Finalize the workflow with the settings that had the lowest cross-validated RMSE. Then `last_fit()` fits it on the whole training set and evaluates it on the test set:

```{r last-fit}
final <- finalize_workflow(wf, select_best(res, metric = "rmse"))
final_fit <- last_fit(final, split)
collect_metrics(final_fit)
```

### Nested cross-validation

To estimate how well the whole tuning process does, use nested cross-validation with the [nestedtune](https://github.com/tidymodels/nestedtune) package, which is in development. Give `nested_resamples()` balanced folds at both levels. The inner folds are made from each outer analysis set, so they are balanced within it. `group` works at both levels too.

```{r nested, eval = FALSE}
library(nestedtune)

nested <- nested_resamples(
  d,
  outside = balanced_vfold_cv(v = 5, balance = c(age, income), exact = site),
  inside = balanced_vfold_cv(v = 5, balance = c(age, income), exact = site)
)
nested_res <- nested_tune_grid(wf, nested, grid = 6)
collect_metrics(nested_res)
```

## Choosing a method

balancedsample has four methods. All of them keep the `exact` counts. They differ in how they make the sets similar on the `balance` columns:

- `"anticlust"` (the default) uses k-plus anticlustering from the [anticlust](https://cran.r-project.org/package=anticlust) package ([Papenberg, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1111/bmsp.12315)). It starts from a random assignment and swaps rows of the same `exact` stratum between sets when the swap improves one score for how similar the means and variances of the sets are. By default, it considers every row of the same stratum as a swap partner, so its run time grows quickly with the number of rows.
- `"twinning"` uses data twinning from the [twinning](https://cran.r-project.org/package=twinning) package ([Vakayil and Joseph, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1002/sam.11574)). It takes one set out of the data at a time. It takes a row and its nearest unused neighbours as a small group and keeps that first row for the set. The next group starts at the unused row closest to the last group's farthest neighbour, so the set covers the data the way the whole data does. It does this within each `exact` stratum. For folds, the default strategy repeats this on the rows that are left. It needs the twinning package, allows only some split proportions, and splits small strata at random (for folds, strata with fewer than `2 * v` rows). Leave the outcome out of `balance` and `exact` with this method (see [Choosing columns](#choosing-columns-balance-and-exact)).
- `"rerandomize"` uses rerandomization ([Morgan and Rubin, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1214/12-AOS1008)). It draws stratified random splits and scores each one by its Mahalanobis imbalance: a distance between the means of the sets that takes the correlations between the columns into account. For folds, the score is the largest imbalance of any fold against the rest. It keeps the first draw that scores under a cutoff, set from 100 pilot draws so that about 10% of draws pass. If none of 1,000 draws passes, it uses the best one, with a warning. It balances means only, and needs no extra package.
- `"interaction"` cuts each numeric column into up to four bins by rank, crosses them with the levels of the categorical columns, and stratifies at random on the result. Within each `exact` stratum, cells with fewer than 10% of all the rows are pooled. Crossed cells get small fast: here, with age and income in quartiles and 9 `exact` strata, the largest cell has 8 rows and the cutoff is 30, so every cell is pooled and the folds are random within the `exact` strata. It is a baseline that shows how crossed strata become sparse.

This compares all four on the full data with 10 folds:

```{r methods}
methods <- c("anticlust", "twinning", "rerandomize", "interaction")
by_method <- lapply(methods, function(m) {
  f <- balanced_vfold_cv(
    d,
    v = 10,
    balance = c(age, income),
    exact = c(diagnosis, site),
    method = m
  )
  s <- summary(balance_check(f))
  data.frame(
    method = m,
    max_abs_smd = max(s$max_abs_smd),
    mean_abs_smd = mean(s$mean_abs_smd),
    mean_energy = mean(s$energy)
  )
})
by_method <- do.call(rbind, by_method)
shown <- by_method
shown[-1] <- round(shown[-1], 3)
shown
```

In this run, the smallest `max_abs_smd` came from `r by_method$method[which.min(by_method$max_abs_smd)]` (`r round(min(by_method$max_abs_smd), 3)`), the smallest `mean_abs_smd` from `r by_method$method[which.min(by_method$mean_abs_smd)]` (`r round(min(by_method$mean_abs_smd), 3)`), and the smallest `mean_energy` from `r by_method$method[which.min(by_method$mean_energy)]` (`r round(min(by_method$mean_energy), 3)`). These come from one run of each method on one data set, so they don't show which method does best in general, and small differences may be noise.

Start with anticlust, but watch its run time on large data. In one test on one computer, with 10 folds and four numeric variables, it took 0.5 seconds for 1,000 rows, 3.7 seconds for 3,000 rows, 25 seconds for 10,000 rows, and 3.6 minutes for 30,000 rows. With `options = list(k_neighbours = 20)`, each row can only swap with its 20 nearest neighbours, and the same runs took 0.3, 1.6, 4.1, and 11.7 seconds. Twinning took under 0.5 seconds for all four sizes. On large data, use `k_neighbours` or twinning, then check the balance again. With `k_neighbours = 20`, look at the categorical columns in particular: in one test with 5,000 rows, their largest SMD rose from about 0.005 to about 0.1, while the numeric columns stayed as well balanced. See `?balanced_vfold_cv` for the options of each method.

## Groups

If the data have several rows per person, put the person ID in `group`. All of a person's rows then go to the same set. Columns in `exact` must be constant within each person, and the exact counts are counts of people, not rows. `group` works the same way in `balanced_initial_split()`.

```{r groups}
d$person <- seq_len(n)
long <- d[rep(seq_len(n), times = sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE)), ]
grouped <- balanced_vfold_cv(
  long,
  v = 5,
  balance = c(age, income),
  exact = c(diagnosis, site),
  group = person
)
grouped
```

The split sizes are numbers of rows. Each fold gets about the same number of people, so the number of rows per fold varies with how many rows each person has. `balance_check()` also compares rows.

To make the split, the method sees each person as one row, with the person's means of the `balance` columns and the log of their number of rows. anticlust has a `must_link` argument for groups. balancedsample does not use it, because it needs fold sizes that the groups can fill exactly, and it was slow in tests.

## References

Bengio, Y., & Grandvalet, Y. (2004). No unbiased estimator of the variance of k-fold cross-validation. *Journal of Machine Learning Research, 5*, 1089-1105.

Diamantidis, N. A., Karlis, D., & Giakoumakis, E. A. (2000). Unsupervised stratification of cross-validation for accuracy estimation. *Artificial Intelligence, 116*(1-2), 1-16.

Joseph, V. R., & Vakayil, A. (2022). SPlit: An optimal method for data splitting. *Technometrics, 64*(2), 166-176.

Kohavi, R. (1995). A study of cross-validation and bootstrap for accuracy estimation and model selection. In *Proceedings of the Fourteenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence* (pp. 1137-1144).

Moreno-Torres, J. G., Sáez, J. A., & Herrera, F. (2012). Study on the impact of partition-induced dataset shift on k-fold cross-validation. *IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems, 23*(8), 1304-1312.

Morgan, K. L., & Rubin, D. B. (2012). Rerandomization to improve covariate balance in experiments. *The Annals of Statistics, 40*(2), 1263-1282.

Papenberg, M. (2024). K-plus anticlustering: An improved k-means criterion for maximizing between-group similarity. *British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 77*(1), 80-102.

Vakayil, A., & Joseph, V. R. (2022). Data twinning. *Statistical Analysis and Data Mining, 15*(5), 598-610.

Zeng, X., & Martinez, T. R. (2000). Distribution-balanced stratified cross-validation for accuracy estimation. *Journal of Experimental & Theoretical Artificial Intelligence, 12*(1), 1-12.
